rendered: The document does not say the EG process corroded the aluminium foil. It reports the opposite: the foil came out without corrosion. The paper states that the aluminum foil was fully recovered without any corrosion[1]. The recovered foils had shiny surfaces, which the authors took to mean that suggesting that no corrosion occurred and that no residues of[2] electrode material remained. Imaging and EDX of the foil support this (Fig. 3[3]). Corrosion is discussed in the paper as a general risk: aluminium foils are reactive and easily subject to corrosion during separation,[4] which can contaminate the active materials. The paper also links corrosion to water-based separation: water is suitable for delamination because the aluminum foil exhibited[5] corrosion due to lithium leaching from the NMC cathode,[6] making the water solution basic.[7] The corrosion would contaminate the cathode because the aluminium forms (OH)3 precipitates on the cathode surfaces.[8] Because no corrosion occurred with EG, the document does not describe any step for removing a corrosion product. The only cleaning steps it describes are washing the electrode in dimethyl carbonate to remove the electrolyte.[9] before delamination, and rinsing the delaminated cathode with alcohol to remove the EG residues.[10] The paper also says the recovered aluminium has no active material left on it.
